title: 📘 UNIT 5: PEOPLES AND STATES OF AFRICA TO 1500
🗣️ 5.1 LANGUAGES AND PEOPLES OF AFRICA
notes:
🌍 Africa has over 1000 diverse and interrelated languages.

⭐ Languages belonging to the same group share certain vocabulary or words.

📚 African peoples are classified according to four major language super-families.

title: 🌐 FOUR LANGUAGE SUPER-FAMILIES
notes:
1️⃣ Congo-Kordofanian

2️⃣ Afro-Asiatic

3️⃣ Nilo-Saharan

4️⃣ Khoisan

title: 🌍 AFRO-ASIATIC SUPER-FAMILY
notes:
📍 Speakers live mainly in northern Africa, the Sahara, the Horn of Africa and around Lake Chad.

⭐ Six sub-groups:
• Berber
• Chadic
• Coptic (Ancient Egyptian)
• Cushitic
• Omotic
• Semitic

title: 🟢 AFRO-ASIATIC: CUSHITIC AND SEMITIC
notes:
⭐ Semitic:
• Spoken mainly in the Horn of Africa.

⭐ Omotic:
• Spoken only in Ethiopia.

⭐ Cushitic:
• Extends from the Red Sea coast through the Horn of Africa into central Kenya and Tanzania.

title: 🟣 NIGER-CONGO LANGUAGE FAMILY
notes:
• Niger-Congo covers much of West Africa and all of Bantu Africa.

• Bantu speakers live across much of sub-Saharan Africa.

• There are over 450 languages grouped in the Bantu family.

• Kiswahili belongs to the Bantu language group.

• Kordofanian languages are spoken in a small area of the Nuba Hills, south of Sudan.

title: 🔵 NILO-SAHARAN SUPER-FAMILY
notes:
⭐ The Nilo-Saharan super-family is divided into six subgroups:

• Chari-Nile
• Songhay
• Saharan
• Meban
• Koman
• Fur

title: 🟤 KHOISAN SUPER-FAMILY
notes:
⭐ Two major subgroups:

• Khoikhoi
• San

📍 Speakers live in and around the Kalahari Desert of northern South Africa, southwestern Botswana and Namibia.

title: ⚠️ LANGUAGES NOT NATIVE TO AFRICA
notes:
• Not all languages spoken in Africa are native to the continent.

• Arabic was brought to Africa by Muslim Arabs between the seventh and eleventh centuries.

• European colonial powers later brought languages such as English, French, Spanish and Portuguese to their African colonies.

title: 🌍 CASE STUDY: LIVING ALONG THE BORDER
notes:
📍 Neima lives in Moyale along the Ethio-Kenyan border.

🗣️ She can communicate in:
• Afan-Oromo
• Amharic
• Somali
• Swahili
• English

💼 She also participates in local trade activities to earn a living.

title: 🏛️ 5.2 STATES IN NORTH AFRICA
notes:
⭐ The section discusses two important states:

• Mamluk Egypt
• Funj Sultanate

title: 🇪🇬 MAMLUK EGYPT
notes:
• Fatimid rulers used soldiers called Mamluks.

• The Mamluks were of Turkish origin.

• They gradually became military commanders and took power militarily.

• They founded a dynasty that ruled Egypt from 1250 to 1517.

title: 🌍 MAMLUK EXPANSION
notes:
• The Mamluks expanded into:
• Palestine
• Syria
• Europe
• Asia

💰 Egypt also experienced important economic developments during Mamluk rule.

title: 🤝 MAMLUKS AND ETHIOPIA
notes:
• Ethio-Egyptian relations were full of conflicts during Mamluk rule.

• Ethiopian ruler Zera Yacob (r. 1434–1468) tried to create smooth relations.

• Their improved relationship was short-lived.

title: 📉 DECLINE OF MAMLUK EGYPT
notes:
⭐ Factors for decline:
• Corruption
• Decline in agricultural productivity
• Cattle plague
• Drought

⚔️ Firearms helped the Ottoman Turks defeat the Mamluk forces in Palestine.

📅 The Ottomans occupied Egypt in 1517.

title: 🐄 FUNJ SULTANATE
notes:
• Established in 1504 by cattle-keeping nomads in northeast Africa, in present-day Sudan.

• Capital was Sennar.

• The Funj fought against the Christian kingdom of Ethiopia because of rivalry over trade routes.

title: ⚔️ FUNJ: RISE AND FALL
notes:
• The army of King Susenyos destroyed the Funj forces around 1620.

• The Funj Sultanate continued to exist afterward.

• Muhammed Ali of Egypt conquered the Funj Sultanate in the 1820s.

title: ☪️ 5.3 SPREAD OF ISLAM AND ITS IMPACT IN WEST AFRICA
notes:
• Islam was born in the early 7th century.

• Muslim Arabs conquered Egypt in 642 AD.

• They later expanded across North Africa.

• By the end of the century, the Arab Empire had reached Morocco and conquered southern Spain.

title: 🌍 ISLAM AND NORTH AFRICA
notes:
• Politico-religious rivalries in the 11th century were followed by a revival of Islam in North Africa.

• A further wave of Arab immigration also took place.

• This was followed by the expansion of West African empires.

title: 🚢 ISLAM AND WEST AFRICAN TRADE
notes:
• Islam promoted trade between West Africa and the Mediterranean.

• It developed and widened the Trans-Saharan caravan trade.

• The trade enriched West African and Muslim traders.

• Muslims from North Africa settled in commercial centers.

title: 🤝 SOCIAL AND CULTURAL IMPACT OF ISLAM
notes:
• Islam linked diverse peoples through better cultural understanding.

• It encouraged a spirit of cooperation and commonwealth.

• Increased trade and wealth helped the rise of great African empires.

title: 👑 ISLAM AND POLITICAL POWER
notes:
• Islam facilitated the rise of political empires that encouraged trade and wealth.

• Kings found Islam attractive because the caliph combined political power with religious authority.

title: 🌍 5.4 STATES IN WESTERN AFRICA
notes:
⭐ Major West African states and empires included:

• Ghana
• Mali
• Songhay
• Kanem-Bornu
• Hausa States

💰 Control of Trans-Saharan trade contributed greatly to their power.

title: 👑 GHANA EMPIRE
notes:
• Located in parts of present-day Mauritania, Mali and Senegal.

• Founded by the Soninke people in the fourth century AD.

• Reached the height of its power around 1000 AD.

• Relied heavily on Trans-Saharan trade.

title: 📉 FALL OF GHANA
notes:
• The rise of Islam was an important factor in the greatness and decline of Ghana.

• Ancient Ghana came to an end in 1076.

• The Almoravids invaded and captured its capital, Kumbi Saleh.

title: 👑 MALI EMPIRE
notes:
• Mali emerged after the fall of Ghana.

• Sundiata Keita founded the Mali Empire of the Mandinka people.

• Mali spread its language, laws and customs along the Niger River.

title: ⭐ MANSA MUSA
notes:
• Mansa Musa was the greatest king of Mali.

• He ruled from 1312 to 1337.

• He made a pilgrimage to Mecca.

• Islam expanded greatly during his reign.

title: 📚 TIMBUKTU AND MALI
notes:
• Mali was famous for Islamic studies.

• Timbuktu became one of the most important Islamic learning and cultural centers.

title: 📉 FALL OF MALI
notes:
• After Mansa Musa, no king was as powerful.

• Mali weakened because of inefficient leadership.

• Attacks from neighboring peoples such as the Tuareg also contributed to its decline.

⭐ Songhai later replaced Mali as an advanced African kingdom.

title: 👑 SONGHAI EMPIRE
notes:
• The Songhai people established an empire named after themselves.

• Its capital was Gao.

• Songhai had previously been subject to Ghana and Mali.

• Toward the end of the 14th century, Songhai ended Mali's overlordship.

title: 🌍 SONGHAI: EXPANSION AND ECONOMY
notes:
• The empire extended from the central area of present-day Nigeria to the Atlantic coast.

• Songhai became powerful by controlling Trans-Saharan trade.

• It had trading connections with the Berbers.

• Prosperity increased as gold came from the forest region.

title: ☪️ SONGHAI AND ISLAM
notes:
• Songhai kings accepted Islam early in the 11th century.

• Islam became an important part of the empire's political and cultural development.

title: 📉 FALL OF SONGHAI
notes:
• Songhai Empire ended in 1591.

• A Moroccan army defeated Songhai at the Battle of Tondibi.

title: 🏛️ KANEM-BORNU
notes:
• Kanem-Bornu was one of the kingdoms in the grassland region of Africa.

• Its ruling family was a Muslim dynasty.

• Trade was important for Kanem's greatness.

• The army protected trade routes and collected taxes from traders.

title: 📉 DECLINE OF KANEM-BORNU
notes:
• After Bornu became a province of Kanem, the empire was often called Kanem-Bornu.

• It probably began to decline because trade centers shifted from inland routes to the Atlantic coast of West Africa.

title: 🏙️ HAUSA CITY-STATES
notes:
• Hausa city-states emerged in Nigeria between 1000 and 1200 AD.

• The people were both pastoralists and farmers.

⭐ Major Hausa states:
• Kano
• Katsina
• Zazzau (Zaria)
• Gobir
• Kebbi
• Rano
• Zamfara

title: 💰 HAUSA ECONOMY AND CULTURE
notes:
• Economy was based on agriculture and Trans-Saharan trade.

• Hausa cities were known for:
• Leather goods
• Craft technology
• Textiles

⭐ Kano was the most famous walled city.

☪️ Islam spread to Hausa land from Kanem-Bornu.

title: 🌍 5.5 EQUATORIAL, CENTRAL AND EASTERN AFRICA
notes:
• Various states and small societies emerged in eastern Africa.

• Islam strongly influenced many of them.

• Some became extremely wealthy through trade.

• Bantu-speaking farming peoples migrated from the Niger River region into East Africa and the Congo River basin.

title: 👑 KINGDOM OF KONGO
notes:
• Located on the lower bank of the Zaire River.

• Founded by Bantu people in the late 14th century.

• The people were hunters, warriors and skilled smiths.

• Agriculture and trade were important to the economy.

title: ✝️ KONGO AND THE PORTUGUESE
notes:
• European explorers reached Kongo in 1482 and 1491.

• Catholic missionaries followed.

• The Portuguese later colonized the kingdom.

title: 🌊 SWAHILI CITY-STATES
notes:
• About 2000 years ago, Bantu-speaking people established small villages along the Indian Ocean coast.

• After the rise of Islam, Muslim Arabic-speaking merchants became influential.

• Some merchants married into local ruling families.

title: 🗣️ SWAHILI LANGUAGE AND CULTURE
notes:
• Swahili developed from interaction between African and Arab cultures.

• The word Swahili means 'coasters' in Arabic.

• Swahili is now a common language in East African countries.

⭐ Swahili Civilization is an example of cultural diffusion.

title: 🏙️ IMPORTANT SWAHILI CITY-STATES
notes:
⭐ Important coastal cities and ports included:

• Mogadishu
• Malindi
• Mombasa
• Zanzibar
• Kilwa
• Brava
• Pate
• Pemba
• Sofala

title: 💰 KILWA AND EAST AFRICAN TRADE
notes:
• Kilwa was the most famous and imposing Swahili city.

• It was situated on a small island.

• Kilwa became the main center of East African gold and ivory trade.

• Wealthy Muslim elites ruled the Swahili cities.

title: 🌍 SWAHILI INTERNATIONAL RELATIONS
notes:
• Swahili cities had commercial relations with:
• Arabia
• Persia
• India
• China

• These relations existed long before the Portuguese arrival.

title: ⚓ PORTUGUESE IN EAST AFRICA
notes:
• The Portuguese aimed to destroy the growing power of Muslims in East Africa.

• They were attracted by East Africa's gold and ivory trade.

• Portugal established a trading fort at Sofala in 1505.

title: 🌍 5.6 SOUTHERN AFRICA
notes:
• States formed more slowly in southern Africa than in the north.

• Independent villages gradually consolidated beginning in the 11th century.

• These groupings eventually formed the first states.

title: 🏛️ GREAT ZIMBABWE
notes:
• Founded by Bantu-speaking Shona people around AD 1000.

• Stone houses and walls were built during the 13th or 14th century.

• Great Zimbabwe was a medieval African city known for its large circular wall and tower.

title: 💰 GREAT ZIMBABWE: ECONOMY
notes:
⭐ Economic activities included:
• Cattle husbandry
• Crop cultivation
• Gold trade

• Great Zimbabwe was the heart of a thriving trading empire from the 11th to the 15th centuries.

• It maintained trade relations with the Swahili states.

title: 👑 MWENE MUTAPA
notes:
• Great Zimbabwe was known for its gold mines.

• After 1450 AD, Rozwi clan kings of the Shona people established the empire called Mwene Mutapa.

• The Portuguese later conquered Mwene Mutapa in the late 16th century.

title: 🐄 THE KHOI-KHOI
notes:
• Initially, the Khoi-Khoi were hunters.

• Since about 1000 AD, they changed from hunting to sheep and cattle breeding.

• Beginning around 1300 AD, they expanded from present-day Botswana.

• They were well established in southern Africa by the 15th century.

title: 📉 KHOI-KHOI AND EUROPEAN SETTLEMENT
notes:
• Dutch settlers landed in South Africa in the mid-17th century.

• The Khoi-Khoi were driven from their land toward the Kalahari Desert.

• Europeans called them Hottentots.

title: 🏹 THE SAN
notes:
• Before European settlement, the San lived in parts of present-day Angola and Namibia.

• Europeans called them Bushmen.

• The San lived mainly by hunting and gathering.

• Men hunted animals with bows and poison-tipped arrows.

title: 🌵 SAN AND THE KALAHARI
notes:
• Dutch farmers pushed the San toward the Kalahari Desert.

• They continued to live as hunters.

• The San speak Khoisan languages characterized by clicking sounds.

⭐ Zimbabwe's name comes from a Shona word meaning 'stone houses'.

title: 🌍 5.7 AFRICA'S INTRA AND INTER-CONTINENTAL RELATIONS
notes:
📌 Intercontinental relation occurs between two or more continents.

📌 Intracontinental relation occurs within a continent.

🌍 African peoples maintained relationships through trade, migration, warfare and exchange of ideas.

title: 🐪 TRANS-SAHARAN CONTACTS
notes:
• Peoples north and south of the Sahara had a long history of irregular contact.

• The introduction of the camel made trade better organized.

• Regular Trans-Saharan caravan trade began in the fourth century.

title: 🤝 IMPACT OF AFRICAN RELATIONS
notes:
• Trade helped develop strong economic and political systems on both sides of the Sahara.

• The spread of Islam strengthened relationships between tropical Africa and North Africa.

• Arab trade with North and East African societies encouraged exchange of ideas.

title: ⚓ AFRICA AND EUROPEAN CONTACT
notes:
• Exploration and contact with European powers contributed to changes in Africa.

• Afro-European contact during the exploration era eventually opened the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade.

title: 🚢 5.8 TRANS-SAHARAN TRADE
notes:
• The exact beginning of Trans-Saharan trade is unknown.

• Two important routes connected West and West-Central Africa with North-Central and North-West Africa.

• These routes linked major ancient and medieval states of West Africa.

title: 🗺️ TRANS-SAHARAN TRADE ROUTES
notes:
⭐ Major routes included:

• Routes connecting West and West-Central Africa with North-Central and North-West Africa.

• A route crossing the central Sahara and connecting North Africa with Kanem.

• A sub-branch connecting West Africa and Egypt.

• The routes also connected Africa with the outside world.

title: 🥇 GOODS OF TRANS-SAHARAN TRADE
notes:
⭐ Important trade goods included:

• Gold from West Africa
• Salt from northwest Africa
• Enslaved people after the emergence of Arabs in the 7th century AD

title: 💰 IMPACT OF TRANS-SAHARAN TRADE
notes:
• Contributed to strong economic and political systems on both sides of the Sahara.

• Helped Ghana, Mali and Songhai become powerful.

• Spread Islam through West and West-Central Africa.

• Increased connections between different African regions.

title: 🌍 5.9 EARLY CONTACTS WITH THE OUTSIDE WORLD
notes:
🌊 East Africa's accessible coast encouraged extensive interaction with outside peoples.

⭐ Early contacts included:
• Arabs
• Greeks
• Persians
• Romans
• Chinese
• Indians
• Spanish
• Portuguese

title: 🇪🇺 EUROPEAN INTEREST IN AFRICA
notes:
• From the mid-15th century, global events brought Africa closer to the rest of the world.

• Portugal and Spain sought to dominate international trade.

• Both countries sponsored navigators and explorers.

title: 🌍 EFFECTS OF EUROPEAN CONTACT
notes:
European exploration and contact contributed to changes in Africa's:

• Economy
• Culture
• Language
• Politics
• Environment

title: ⚠️ TRANS-ATLANTIC SLAVE TRADE
notes: • One major outcome of Afro-European contact during the exploration era was the opening of the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade.
